mechanisms.name: Amyloid Beta Accumulation and Plaque Formation
mechanisms.description: Alzheimer’s disease is centrally characterized by the pathological accumulation of amyloid beta (Aβ) peptides, particularly Aβ42, in the brain. These peptides aggregate to form insoluble plaques, which disrupt neuronal communication and trigger a cascade of neurotoxic events, including oxidative stress, inflammation, and synaptic dysfunction. In ADNI data, this process is reflected by reduced CSF Aβ42 levels and increased amyloid tracer uptake on PET imaging.
mechanisms.label: Amyloid Pathology

mechanisms.name: Tau Pathology and Neurofibrillary Tangle Formation
mechanisms.description: Hyperphosphorylation of tau proteins leads to the formation of neurofibrillary tangles inside neurons. These tangles destabilize microtubules, impair axonal transport, and ultimately result in cell death. Elevated levels of total tau (TAU) and phosphorylated tau (PTAU) in CSF are hallmark biomarkers in AD, indicating ongoing neurodegeneration and correlating with cognitive impairment.
mechanisms.label: Tau Pathology

mechanisms.name: Neurodegeneration and Brain Atrophy
mechanisms.description: Progressive loss of neurons and synapses results in atrophy of specific brain regions implicated in AD. This includes early atrophy in the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex, as well as widespread atrophy in the temporal, parietal, and whole brain regions as disease advances. These structural changes, which are detectable by MRI measures like ventricular enlargement and decreased regional brain volumes, underpin clinical symptoms of memory loss and cognitive decline.
mechanisms.label: Neurodegenerative

mechanisms.name: Glucose Hypometabolism and Synaptic Dysfunction
mechanisms.description: Reduced neuronal and synaptic activity in the AD brain is observed as hypometabolism, particularly in temporoparietal and posterior cingulate cortices. This metabolic impairment is captured by FDG-PET imaging showing reduced glucose uptake and is closely associated with ongoing cognitive and functional decline in AD patients.
mechanisms.label: Metabolic

mechanisms.name: Cognitive Decline and Executive Dysfunction
mechanisms.description: Clinical progression of AD is manifested by a continuum of global cognitive impairment, episodic memory loss, language difficulties, visuospatial deficits, and executive dysfunction. Clinical and neuropsychological tests (e.g., MMSE, MoCA, AVLT, Digit Span, category fluency, Trail Making, ADAS-Cog) assess the severity and domain-specific aspects of cognitive decline reflected in baseline diagnosis.
mechanisms.label: Cognitive

mechanisms.name: Neuropsychiatric and Behavioral Changes
mechanisms.description: AD is often accompanied by neuropsychiatric symptoms such as depression, agitation, irritability, apathy, hallucinations, and sleep disturbances. These behavioral changes, assessed by NPI-Q, GDS, and CDR, significantly impact quality of life and may precede or accompany cognitive impairment. Their presence often reflects the involvement of frontal and limbic structures in the disease.
mechanisms.label: Neuropsychiatric

mechanisms.name: Functional Decline in Daily Living
mechanisms.description: Functional impairment in activities of daily living is a key clinical hallmark as AD progresses from MCI to dementia. This includes difficulties in memory, language, planning, organization, and attention. Both self-reported and informant-based Everyday Cognition (Ecog) scores, as well as the Functional Activities Questionnaire (FAQ), capture these real-world deficits and are crucial for staging disease severity.
mechanisms.label: Functional

mechanisms.name: Vascular and Cardiometabolic Risk Factors
mechanisms.description: Vascular pathology, including hypertension and metabolic syndrome, increases risk for AD, possibly via reduced cerebral perfusion, microvascular injury, and facilitation of amyloid and tau pathology. Continuous variables such as blood pressure, weight, and height contribute to the assessment of vascular health and help distinguish vascular dementia comorbidity.
mechanisms.label: Vascular

mechanisms.name: Demographic and Genetic Susceptibility
mechanisms.description: Age remains the strongest risk factor for AD. Other socio-demographic variables (education, gender, ethnicity, marital status, race) modulate risk and disease manifestation, both through genetic predisposition and environmental/lifestyle factors. Lower education may decrease cognitive reserve, increasing vulnerability to symptomatic AD. Diverse demographic data help identify at-risk groups, inform stratification, and address population differences in AD susceptibility.
mechanisms.label: Risk Factors
